title: Arrested (Acts 21–22)
hook: a riot in the Temple and Paul tells his own story

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farewell on the beach at Miletus. Your line was coveted no one's silver.

Paul reaches Jerusalem. Friends along the way had begged him not to go. A prophet named Agabus even tied his own hands and feet with Paul's belt to show what was coming. Paul went anyway. In Jerusalem, James and the elders welcome him, and to show he still honors the Law, Paul goes to the Temple to be purified with four men under a vow. He's a Jew, worshiping in the Temple of his people. And that's where it all breaks loose.
screen: `AGABUS AND THE BELT.` → `PAUL GOES ANYWAY.` → `TO THE TEMPLE, TO KEEP A VOW.`

segments.voice: Some visitors from Asia see Paul in the Temple and shout that he has brought Greeks into the holy place. He hadn't. They'd seen him in the city earlier with Trophimus, a Gentile from Ephesus, and assumed. The crowd seizes Paul, drags him out, and the gates are shut. They're trying to kill him when word reaches the Roman commander of the garrison, who runs down with soldiers. The beating stops. Paul is chained and carried up the steps of the barracks, the crowd is so violent. At the top of the steps, bruised and in chains, Paul asks to speak. The commander is surprised he speaks Greek. Paul says he is a Jew of Tarsus in Cilicia, in the Douay-Rheims, "a citizen of no mean city." Then he turns and speaks to the crowd in their own language, Hebrew or Aramaic, and they fall quiet. What does he say? Not an argument. His story. I was brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel. I persecuted this Way. On the road to Damascus a light shone around me, and I heard a voice: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" Then a devout man named Ananias came and said, Brother Saul, look up. That's all: what happened to him. They listen, until he says the Lord sent him to the Gentiles. Then the uproar starts again. Later, about to be flogged, Paul quietly asks the centurion whether it's lawful to scourge a Roman citizen who hasn't been condemned. It isn't. The flogging stops.
screen: `A RUMOR IN THE TEMPLE.` · `CHAINED ON THE BARRACKS STEPS.` · `A JEW OF TARSUS, ASKING TO SPEAK.` · `SAUL, SAUL, WHY PERSECUTEST THOU ME?` · then, large: `HE TELLS WHAT HAPPENED.`

segments.voice: If someone asked why you're on this path, practicing, listening, whatever brought you here, what would you say? Not an argument, just what happened: who you were before, one moment that changed something, where you are now, in three short sentences in your head. It doesn't have to be dramatic, and if you pray, thank God for one moment in it.
Arrested. Paul, seized in the Temple over a rumor, rescued by Roman soldiers, and given the steps of a barracks to tell his own story. Today's word.
Your line: tell what happened. A quiet story told honestly is still yours. That's day five hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: In Catholic parishes, adults entering the Church often share their faith story with sponsors and the community during their preparation, and Catholics speak of giving witness by telling plainly what God has done in their lives.

fork.setup: you're Paul, chained, bruised, carried up the barracks steps away from a furious crowd. what do you do?
options: stay quiet and let the soldiers take you in.
ask to speak to the crowd, and tell them your story.

fork.reveal: he asks to speak, the crowd falls silent, and he tells them in their own language what happened to him. he mentions his citizenship only later, when they're about to flog him.

original.note: Greek: in the Hebrew tongue, how Paul addressed the crowd. scholars think it means Aramaic, the everyday language.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul was arrested for preaching Jesus.
what it means: a false rumor sets off a riot, and Paul, in chains, uses his moment not to argue but to tell what happened to him.
what a scholar hears: this is the second of three tellings of Paul's conversion in Acts. Roman law forbade flogging an uncondemned citizen, which is why the centurion stops cold.
recall: I am he: Jesus in the garden

chat.says: When Paul was seized in Jerusalem, how did he defend himself?
options: From the barracks steps he told the crowd his story: who he was, the road, Ananias.
He argued the Law line by line until the whole crowd agreed he was right.
He stayed silent and let the Roman commander speak in his defense.
chat.meaning: Paul didn't argue. In the crowd's own language he told what happened: brought up under Gamaliel, the persecutor, the light on the road, and Ananias.

Agabus.meaning: a prophet who tied himself with Paul's belt

Trophimus.meaning: a Gentile from Ephesus seen with Paul in the city

Cilicia.meaning: the region where Paul's city, Tarsus, stood

Gamaliel.meaning: the teacher Paul was brought up under

notes: Confirm KJV wording of Acts 21:39 and 22:7.
'Brother Saul, receive thy sight' (22:13) is given without quotation marks as a near-paraphrase; confirm.
The framing emphasizes a rumor and avoids blaming 'the Jews'; Paul is himself a Jew worshiping in the Temple. A Keeper should confirm the tone.
'Hebrew dialect' commonly understood as Aramaic: confirm.
Roman citizens' protection from flogging (Lex Porcia / Lex Julia): confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS: Acts 21:39 was quoted from the KJV; now the Douay-Rheims, verified; 22:7 is identical in both and its source now names the Douay. Ananias's words follow Douay 22:13 ('Brother Saul, look up') instead of the KJV's 'receive thy sight'. Cut the stock line 'Rumors move faster than facts'; the vow now follows 21:23–26.
